text: Each map holds 537 bomb hits. One is pure chance, the other follows a rule. Which is chance? Both are simulated. The question isn't. In 1944, Londoners claimed flying bombs fell in clusters, and precise aim would put factories at risk. Build the detector your eye is running. Cut each map into 576 squares, and flag any square with three or more hits, like this one. Map A lights up with 39 targets, map B with none. So A looks aimed. Backwards. I dropped every hit on map A at random, so all 39 targets are false alarms. Map B's rule, no two hits closer than 4 fifths of a square. Your eye expects chance to look that even. Take one square. Each bomb lands in it with chance 1 in 576. To stay empty, all 537 must miss. Guess how many squares stay empty? About 227. Map A has 222. Those empty squares force the clumps. The other 354 share all the hits. So many must double up. To judge London, chance must predict every bar. Call the average hits per square lambda. One minus a small slice, raised to a big power, is almost exactly e to the minus lambda. For two hits in this square, pick two bombs. 537 times 536 ways over two since order doesn matter Each lands with chance one in 576 and the rest miss E to the minus lambda again 536 is almost 537 For three hits each two becomes a 3 For any k a k The powers merge into lambda to the k, the Poisson distribution. Times 576 squares, it It predicts these purple bars. The honest detector compares whole histograms. 39 targets and chance predicts 39. The chi-squared misfit squares each bar's gap and divides by chance's bar. So a miss on a short bar counts more. Map A scores 2.0. Three in four simulated chance maps score worse. That share P is .74. Step B, half the expected empty squares, a tower of single hits, misfit 272. A pattern this even is the fingerprint of a spacing rule. Aimed bombs would miss the other way. Extra empty squares, extra pileups. In 1946, R. D. Clarke published the same test on London's real hits. 537 in 576 squares. predicted 227 empty squares. Clark counted 229. Overall, p equals 0.88. The bombs were aimed at central London, but tended to fall short, so farther north, hits were about half as dense. The test needs one lambda. Clark chose an area where it held steady. So look again. Map ace clumps are what no aim at all looks like. If you chose map b, you chose the rule.
